pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Global Wind Patterns for ages 11–13 — the planet-scale engine that organises wind into bands: three circulation cells per hemisphere, the surface trade winds/westerlies/polar easterlies they produce, the Coriolis deflection that bends them, and the high-altitude jet streams.
• Standards — UK: KS3 geography 'weather and climate' / 'atmospheric circulation' and links to KS3 science 'Energy' (uneven heating drives convection). Foundational for GCSE geography global atmospheric circulation and climate zones.
• Standards — US: NGSS MS-ESS2-6 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-6, MS-PS1-5]). DCI ESS2.C, ESS2.D.
• Operational details: build from the child's known idea that warm air rises (local convection) to the GLOBAL case — intense heating at the equator drives rising air that would flow in one giant loop except the planet's rotation breaks it into three cells (Hadley, Ferrel, polar); introduce Coriolis as APPARENT deflection due to rotation (right in N hemisphere, left in S), not a real sideways force; connect cells→surface wind belts→why deserts sit at ~30° and rainforests at the equator; add the jet stream and its waviness/Arctic-amplification as an extension.
• Checkpoint: [Tier B] child can explain that the equator gets more direct sunlight, warm air rises there and sinks near 30°, creating predictable wind belts, and that Earth's spin bends the winds; [Tier C] child can name the three cells, predict wind direction with Coriolis, and link cell descending/ascending branches to desert and rainforest locations.
bestPractices: Start from what they own — warm air rises, cool air sinks (convection they've felt over a radiator) — then scale it to the planet: the equator is heated most, so a giant convection loop wants to form; show why one loop breaks into three cells once rotation is added.

Teach Coriolis as an APPARENT deflection arising from observing motion on a rotating sphere, not a push. The classic demo: draw a straight line 'poleward' on a spinning disc/globe and watch it curve; winds deflect right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern.

Link the cells causally to what children can check on a map: rising air at the equator → clouds and rainforest; descending dry air at ~30° → the world's great deserts (Sahara, Australian); this makes the abstract circulation predict real geography.

Name the surface belts as the OUTPUT of the cells: trade winds (equatorward, easterly), mid-latitude westerlies, polar easterlies — and connect the westerlies to why weather in the UK/US generally moves west-to-east.

Extend to the jet streams as fast high-altitude rivers of air at cell boundaries; for older/able pupils introduce Rossby-wave waviness and the debated link between a warming Arctic and a wavier, more stuck jet stream — flagged as active science, not settled fact.
keyRepresentations: The three-cell cross-section: a hemisphere in profile showing Hadley (0–30°), Ferrel (30–60°) and polar (60–90°) cells with rising/sinking arrows and the surface wind belts beneath.
Rotating-globe/spinning-disc Coriolis demo: a straight-intended path curving into an arc, showing right-deflection (N) and left-deflection (S).
Global wind-belt map: trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies drawn as arrows over the real continents, aligned with equatorial rainforests and 30° deserts.
Jet-stream ribbon on a polar-view globe, shown both as a tidy circle and as a wavy meandering path.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the Coriolis effect is a real sideways force pushing the air, rather than an apparent deflection from viewing motion on a spinning planet (and the myth that it determines which way sinks/toilets drain — far too small at that scale).
Believing air simply flows in one straight loop from equator to pole; missing that rotation splits it into three cells per hemisphere.
Assuming winds are named for where they blow TO; in fact winds are named for the direction they come FROM (a 'westerly' blows from the west).
Thinking the equator is hottest because it is closer to the Sun, rather than because sunlight strikes it more directly (higher angle, energy concentrated over less area).
Treating deserts as random hot places rather than the predictable result of descending dry air in the subtropical high-pressure belts at ~30°.

learn.summary: Global wind patterns for ages 11–13: how uneven solar heating plus Earth's rotation together produce the three circulation cells per hemisphere (Hadley 0–30°, Ferrel 30–60°, polar 60–90°), the surface wind belts they generate (trade winds, mid-latitude westerlies, polar easterlies), the apparent Coriolis deflection (rightward in the Northern Hemisphere, leftward in the Southern), and the high-altitude jet stream that steers weather systems along it. Core target is NGSS MS-ESS2-6 'develop and use a model': build the pattern from two drivers (heating contrast and spin) rather than only labelling a finished diagram, and connect descending dry air at ~30° to the world's great deserts and rising equatorial air to rainforests, with jet-stream waviness/Arctic amplification as a debated extension linked to prolonged extreme weather.

activities.title: Build the planet's circulation from two dials: heating and spin
feedback: If the learner expects one loop from equator to pole: increase the spin dial and watch the loop fragment into three cells — rotation is what breaks the simple picture.

If the learner thinks a parcel curves because something pushes it sideways: note that the parcel travels nearly straight while the ground rotates beneath it; the curved trace is how that looks from our spinning frame.
When the map is overlaid, prompt: where does the descending dry branch land? Connecting ~30° sinking air to real deserts shows the deserts are predictable, not random.
If the learner confuses which way winds bend: compare a Northern-Hemisphere launch (curves right) with a Southern-Hemisphere launch (curves left).

On the jet-stream extension: prompt how a wavier, more 'stuck' jet stream could let a heatwave or cold snap persist much longer by holding a weather pattern in place — and flag the Arctic-amplification link as debated, active science rather than settled fact.
activities.rationale: The objective is to develop and use a model of how unequal heating and rotation cause circulation patterns; manipulating the two drivers and seeing the belts emerge targets that performance expectation directly, and building from the familiar 'warm air rises' convection the learner already owns scaffolds the global case. Sliders, the parcel-launch tool, and the map overlay are optional concrete mechanisms that make the causal relationship manipulable rather than merely labelled.
sourceClaims: Unequal heating of Earth's surface and the planet's rotation together produce large-scale [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-6] — the target of a develop-and-use-a-model performance expectation.

Global circulation is organised into three cells per hemisphere (Hadley 0–30°, Ferrel 30–60°, polar 60–90°), producing surface trade winds, mid-latitude westerlies and polar easterlies; subtropical descending air at ~30° creates the major desert belts.
learnerActions: Starting with the planet's spin set to zero, increase the equator-to-pole heating contrast and observe a single giant convection loop per hemisphere form: warm air rising at the equator, drifting poleward aloft, sinking, and returning along the surface.

Now increase the spin dial up to Earth's rotation rate and observe the single loop break into three side-by-side cells per hemisphere, arranged by latitude, with surface wind belts drawn beneath (trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies).
Use a 'launch a parcel' tool to fire a puff of air poleward and watch its path curve — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern.
Slide a real world map underneath and check where the circulation's branches land: rising equatorial air over the rainforests, descending ~30° air over the Sahara and Australian deserts.

As an extension, toggle a jet-stream ribbon at a cell boundary and observe how this fast high-altitude river of air steers weather systems along its path; then explore a 'wavier jet' slider and reason about what a more meandering, 'stuck' jet might do to the weather beneath it.
activities.intendedInsight: Large-scale wind bands are the emergent OUTPUT of two interacting drivers — uneven heating by latitude and the planet's rotation. The single convection loop you expect splits into three cells once spin is added, and the bending of the winds is an apparent deflection that only appears once the planet turns beneath the moving air, not a sideways push.

activities.title: Spin a globe and launch parcels across it (spatial Coriolis)
feedback: If the learner predicts a straight trace, or a curve 'because a force bends it': point out that no sideways push is applied — the disc or globe rotates beneath the straight-moving pen, so the trace curves.
If the learner cannot say why the hemispheres differ: have them view the spin from above each pole and notice the rotation appears opposite, which flips the apparent deflection.
activities.rationale: Coriolis is a spatial, frame-dependent phenomenon; a spinnable globe or turntable offers a different, hands-on experience of the same idea the 2D lab shows, and either can support the intuition. This is a complementary route to the spatial understanding, not a claim that 3D is required.
sourceClaims: The Coriolis effect is an apparent deflection of moving air (to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern) arising from Earth's rotation, not a real applied force; it is negligible at small scales such as draining sinks.
learnerActions: On a spinnable 3D globe, launch a 'straight' path from the equator toward a pole and watch the trace curve relative to the rotating surface: in both hemispheres, a parcel moving toward the pole arcs eastward. On a physical turntable/lazy-Susan, which stands for one hemisphere seen from above its pole, draw a straight line with a pen across the spinning disc and watch the trace curve.
Compare launches in the Northern Hemisphere (path curves right) and the Southern Hemisphere (path curves left), and say why the two differ.
Peel back or tilt to view the three cells as latitude bands girdling the planet, and view the jet stream as a meandering ribbon from a polar vantage.
activities.intendedInsight: Circulation wraps a rotating sphere; seeing a straight-intended path curve on a surface you can spin makes the apparent (frame-dependent) nature of Coriolis concrete, and the opposite deflection in each hemisphere follows from the direction of rotation seen from each pole.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, sequence, predict, and locate
feedback: If a learner names a wind for where it blows TO: remind them winds are named for the direction they come FROM — a 'westerly' blows from the west.
If a learner says the equator is hottest because it is nearer the Sun: refocus on the angle of incidence — direct rays concentrate energy over a smaller area.
If a learner treats deserts as randomly placed hot spots: trace them to descending dry air in the subtropical high-pressure belts at ~30°.
If a learner cannot say why UK/US weather tends to arrive from the west: link it to the prevailing mid-latitude westerlies, which blow from west to east.
activities.rationale: Recognition and recall tasks are well suited to consolidating specific discriminations and are best used after the model has been explored, since recognition-format responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the model.
learnerActions: Match each cell to its latitude band (Hadley 0–30°, Ferrel 30–60°, polar 60–90°) and each surface belt to its wind direction (trade winds easterly/equatorward, mid-latitude westerlies, polar easterlies).
Sequence the causal chain: equator heated most → air rises → drifts poleward → sinks near 30° → returns as surface wind belt.
Given a poleward-launched parcel, draw or select its correctly curved path in each hemisphere (right in N, left in S).
Categorise named regions as wet-equatorial (rising air) or dry-subtropical (descending air at ~30°), e.g. placing the Sahara and Australian deserts under descending air.
Explain in your own words why the equator is hottest — sunlight strikes it more directly, concentrating energy over less area — rather than because it is closer to the Sun.
Connect the mid-latitude westerlies to everyday experience: because they blow from the west, weather systems in the UK and US generally move from west to east.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure the discriminations after exploring the model: naming cells and belts, predicting deflection direction, locating deserts/rainforests from the circulation, and linking the westerlies to west-to-east weather turn the model into reliable, transferable knowledge.

activities.title: Ask the meteorologist: untangle Coriolis and wind-naming
feedback: If the learner invokes a sideways force: steer back to the rotating-frame account — the air moves nearly straight while the ground turns beneath it.

If the learner cites the plughole myth: note that at that scale the basin's shape and any leftover swirl in the water decide the spin direction; Coriolis matters only over large distances and long times.

If the learner says winds blow straight from high pressure to low pressure: the pressure difference starts the flow, but for large-scale winds rotation then curves it, so they do not travel in a straight line from high to low pressure. Near the equator and in small local winds such as sea breezes, this curving is weak.
activities.rationale: Responsive dialogue is a useful supporting probe for persistent verbal misconceptions, complementing the model work; it targets explanation and misconception repair rather than the emergent spatial system itself.
learnerActions: Pose and discuss whether the Coriolis effect is a real push on the air, and explain in your own words what actually makes a north-bound wind veer right in the Northern Hemisphere.
Ask why 'a westerly' is named for where the wind comes from, and check the drain/toilet-spin claim against the fact that Coriolis is negligible at small scales.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the explanation aloud and responding to follow-up questions can expose and help repair the Coriolis-as-force and winds-named-from misconceptions that a diagram may leave hidden.

constraints: Build from the learner's existing 'warm air rises, cool air sinks' convection idea before scaling to the global case; the single-loop-then-three-cells progression matters for understanding WHY rotation changes the picture.
Teach Coriolis as an apparent (frame-dependent) deflection, not a real sideways force, and explicitly correct the plughole/toilet-drain myth as too small a scale for Coriolis to dominate.
Winds are named for the direction they come FROM, not where they blow to.

A static labelled cross-section or wind-belt map is a useful summary/reference but does not let the learner generate the pattern from its two drivers; use it alongside, not instead of, the manipulable model.

A turntable or an on-screen globe are physical or modelled approximations; name the screen model as a model, and treat the pen-on-disc demo as an analogy for the atmosphere's frame-dependent deflection, not an exact replica.
Recognition and matching tasks consolidate discriminations but do not by themselves require the learner to independently construct or explain the model; pair them with explanation tasks.
Treat the Arctic-amplification / wavier-jet-stream link as active, debated science flagged as an extension, not as settled fact.

Climate connections (deserts at ~30°, equatorial rainforests, westerlies steering UK/US weather west-to-east) describe the dominant large-scale pattern; local geography and other factors also shape real regional climates.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all four sources carry verified:false in the row and were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated or tested interventions.

Source claims support the underlying science principles (NGSS target, three-cell structure, Coriolis as apparent deflection) but do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular activity format or medium; sourceClaims on the consolidation and conversation activities were set to [] because no source supports their pedagogical rationales.

The original row asserted that a static image 'can label but not let the child generate' the causal relationship and that 3D 'adds real depth the 2D cross-section can't'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances (static image as reference/summary; globe as a complementary spatial route).

The jet-stream waviness / Arctic-amplification link was flagged in the source as debated active science; retained only as an extension, now including the objective's link to prolonged extreme weather and the jet's steering role, with the 'debated' caveat preserved.

The pen-on-turntable demo is an analogy (a horizontally moving pen on a flat disc) rather than a full physical model of poleward atmospheric motion — kept as a demonstration of the frame-dependent effect, not an exact atmospheric replica.

assess.poeTask: Set a turntable (or lazy-Susan) spinning and hold a pen still, moving it in a straight line across the spinning disc. Before doing it, ask the student to PREDICT what line the pen leaves ON the disc, and WHY. The reason — the disc rotates beneath the straight-moving pen so the trace curves even though no force acts sideways on the pen — is the diagnostic part; a student who predicts a straight line, or who predicts a curve 'because a force bends it,' reveals the Coriolis-as-force misconception.
probeDeeper: On a merry-go-round you roll a ball straight across and it seems to curve. How is that the same as the wind's deflection?
The Coriolis deflection is rightward in the Northern Hemisphere. What happens in the Southern Hemisphere, and why the difference?
How could a wavier jet stream make a heatwave or cold snap last much longer?
assess.correctAnswer: There's no real sideways force pushing the air. The air moves nearly straight, but the Earth rotates beneath it; from our rotating frame the path appears deflected — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. It's an apparent deflection due to Earth's rotation, not a force acting on the air. Combined with unequal heating by latitude, this shapes the three-cell circulation and the prevailing winds.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The Coriolis force physically pushes the moving air sideways'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Spin a globe/turntable and draw a 'straight' line — the trace curves with no push applied.
errorPatterns.distractor: A real sideways force pushes the wind and makes it curve.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names a real sideways force acting on the air

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Winds blow in a straight line directly from high pressure to low pressure'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The pressure gradient starts the flow; rotation then curves it (qualitative geostrophic balance).
errorPatterns.distractor: Winds go straight from high pressure to low pressure.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The Coriolis effect decides which way water spins down a plughole or toilet'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Too small a scale — basin shape dominates; Coriolis matters only over large distances.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cites the drain myth as evidence

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Global winds are just local breezes scaled up, nothing to do with latitude cells'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link unequal heating by latitude to the Hadley/Ferrel/polar cells.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: no three-cell structure; can't tie winds to latitude

responseLevels.gap: Treats Coriolis as a real push, or has winds going straight from high to low pressure.
responseLevels.full: Explains Coriolis as an apparent deflection from Earth's rotation (not a force), links unequal heating and rotation to the three-cell circulation, prevailing winds and jet stream, and reasons about jet-stream waviness prolonging extreme weather.
responseLevels.partial: Knows winds curve and names the cells or prevailing winds but explains the curving as a force, or can't connect unequal heating → three-cell circulation → surface winds.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Winds don't travel in straight lines from the equator to the poles — they curve. A student says 'that's because the Coriolis force pushes the moving air sideways.' Is the Coriolis effect a real push on the air, and what actually makes a north-bound wind in the Northern Hemisphere veer to the right?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who treats Coriolis as a physical force gives a different account from one who explains it as an apparent deflection that arises because the ground rotates under the moving air.
